blocks.text: Gesner, who maintains with most of the more recent interpreters that שפן is the rabbit, answers the first objection by saying that he caught rabbits chewing after their meal, half an hour after the food had been given them. And it would be vain to object with what we cited from the Porta coeli. For the scribes corrupted the passage by wrongly inserting a negation into the text, against the intention of the author. It is not credible that he was so foolish as to deny that השפן והארנבת ruminate. For he would then be expressly denying what Moses expressly asserts in Levit. XI, 6. and Deut. XIV, 7., and he would be charging the divinely inspired (θεοπνεύστῳ [theopneustō]) writer with falsehood. The negation אין must therefore be removed. This is further shown by the whole sequence of the passage, which, if you take away the negation, will run as follows: There are animals which ruminate, and others which do not ruminate. The reason is that those which ruminate have no upper teeth except molars. Therefore they cannot cut up their food at one time. And the stomach cannot receive it complete until it has been ground a second time. Hence they have a double crop: an upper one, into which the food descends the first time, and a lower one, by which it is received after it has been [II, 412] ground the second time. אך השפן והארנבת מעלה גרה ויש להם שינים למעלה אבל שיניהם הם חדות מאד ולא יוכלו לטחון האוכל היטב והגמל יש לו שינים [col. 1004] למעלה אבל הם קטנות וחלושות Nevertheless the rabbit and the hare ruminate, although they have upper teeth. But their teeth are very sharp and cannot grind the food perfectly. The camel also has upper teeth, but small and weak.

To the second objection Gesner gives some sort of answer, but very hesitantly. Someone may doubt, he says, whether the sephanim are rabbits, since, as far as I know, these do not usually live among rocks or in rocky places, because they are prevented from digging there, but rather in earthy ground, etc. But since among rocks on hills certain caves or long passages are found which are suitable as dens for rabbits, it should be asked whether in other regions rabbits also usually live in these. Nor is a certain Spaniard, whom Gesner consulted on this matter, much more certain: Among us rabbits are very plentiful in mountainous places and on steep mountains. And I have no doubt that they have underground passages in rougher and stony places, although I have never observed it closely. Again: I once took part in a rabbit hunt in a mountainous place full of rocks, among which I saw little burrows dug out; but whether in the inner parts there was rock or softer earth, I cannot affirm. Nor is it more to the point that Papire Masson writes in his Descriptio Franciae per flumina that little hares, that is, rabbits, almost without number are bred on the island of Calonesus off the Armorican coast, although it is entirely rock and has only its surface covered with earth. This, I say, is not to the point, because the rabbits can stay in that earthy surface and have no need to hollow out the rock beneath it. But one should consult Pierre Quiqueran de Beaujeu in his description of Provence, from which Camerarius quotes these things in his Historiae vol. 2, book 5, ch. 20.

There remains the third objection, which takes more effort to refute, since the ancients state so plainly that the rabbit was an animal formerly peculiar to Spain. This is why, of the Greeks, only the Massilians, who live almost on the border of Spain, knew it. This argument therefore makes me somewhat doubtful whether שפן is really the rabbit. I think the question should be examined further, and that we should not rely on the masters of the Hebrews but rather consult the older interpreters, although they are not consistent with one another, so that it is very difficult to extract the truth from them. I pass over the Chaldee versions, the Syriac and the Samaritan, because for the Hebrew שפן they use words that are entirely unknown. For no one knows what טפזא taphza is in Onkelos, for which Jonathan reads טווזא tauza, and the Samaritan [?] taphsa, except that it seems to be a leaping (ἁλτικὸν [haltikon]) animal, because טפז tephaz in Chaldee and Syriac means to leap or to jump up. Nor is the Syriac ܚܓܣܐ chagasa better known, whose plural חגסי chagase the Chaldee also uses for שפנים sephanim, Prov. XXX, 26. But the Ethiopic ሰጊሔ፡ legiche, [II, 413] Psal. CIII. (in the Hebrew CIV,) 19., I think should be rendered hares, because it corresponds to the Greek τοῖς λαγωοῖς [tois lagōois]. The Arabs, following the same, have الارنب [al-arnab] hares. But the same translators have something else in Proverbs, namely القنافد [al-qanāfid] hedgehogs. And in the Law something else again: there, for השפן, one has الوبر [al-wabr] alwebro, and another الفنك [al-fanak] alpheneco.
